extracted.intended_audience: stand-up comedians (open-mic participants through working pros) seeking coaching/practice guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Practical coaching guidance and an actionable rubric for stand-up comics about how often to perform, what rooms to work, how to track material, how to avoid hack, career tiers, and how to treat bombs. Aimed at advancing from open-micing toward professional work.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-stage time (frequency) thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Three sets a week minimum to develop. Five sets a week to grow. Seven+ sets a week to professionalize. Below three: hobbyist trajectory regardless of talent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage time is the primary currency — track weekly set counts and aim to progress up the thresholds. The explicit numeric targets are: 3+ sets/week (minimum), ~5/week (growth), 7+ (professionalization). Falling below three sets/week will generally keep you in a hobbyist trajectory regardless of natural ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotate across different room types
rubrics_metrics.description: A working comic should hit all four room types: bringer rooms, open mics with comics, bar shows, and booked club shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each room type provides different data: bringer rooms (friends laugh — bad data), open mics with comics (jaded crowd — useful for premise testing), bar shows (civilians but distracted — tests ENERGY and projection), booked club shows (civilians + ticket-buyers — closest to professional conditions). Intentionally schedule sets in each room type so you get varied, actionable feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a structured notebook/archive
rubrics_metrics.description: Date every entry. Premises in one section. Punchlines/tags in another. Bombs and diagnoses in a third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A notebook is your archive: consistently date entries and separate content by function (premises vs punchlines/tags vs bombs/diagnoses). The post emphasizes: 'A comic without a notebook is a comic without an archive.' Use it to track evolution, diagnose failures, and preserve ideas for future fresh angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid or freshen 'hack' premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Hack premises are dead because audiences have heard the punchline a hundred times, the premise no longer reflects current reality, or the comic doesn't actually believe it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a rotating list of currently-hack subjects (e.g., TSA agents, 'smartphones make us antisocial,' 'kids these days,' airplane food, marriage-as-suffering). These premises CAN be salvaged but only with a fresh, specific angle; the bar for salvage is high. Use belief, specificity, and up-to-date reality-checks to judge whether a premise is hack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress through the five tiers of comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Five tiers: 1) Open Micer (free, anywhere). 2) Bringer (paid in venue access). 3) Show Booker (paid in spots). 4) Working Pro (paid in money). 5) Headliner (paid + draws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Career advancement should come from sustained excellence rather than networking alone. Use the tier definitions to benchmark where you are and set practical goals (e.g., move from open-micer to paid spots via consistent performance and material improvement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat bombs as data, not crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Are you treating bombs as data, not crisis?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reframe failures: log bombs in your notebook with diagnoses, analyze what went wrong (premise, timing, energy, room mismatch), and use them to iterate material rather than viewing them as catastrophes. This is explicit in the Working Rubric as a required habit for development.
